query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy, the rapid cooling (or other non-equilibrium processing) produces a supersaturated solid solution that, upon moderate thermal aging (or service exposure), undergoes elemental partitioning. This leads to the nucleation and growth of discrete, Mg‐rich intermetallic precipitates—particularly at grain boundaries—which induce localized galvanic couples that accelerate corrosion at ambient temperatures while simultaneously serving as effective nucleation sites for protective oxide formation during high-temperature exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast, metastable high-entropy alloy with a supersaturated solid solution of Mg and other alloying elements, with density below 6 g/cm³.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal aging or exposure to simulated service temperatures that promote elemental partitioning without full homogenization.
generation.conditions: Processing conditions below complete homogenization; density below 6 g/cm³; aging temperatures sufficient to drive Mg partitioning but not high enough for bulk phase equilibrium.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates, particularly at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Moderate thermal exposure triggers diffusion-controlled partitioning of Mg out of the supersaturated solution, forming discrete intermetallic phases. At room temperature, these precipitates create local galvanic couples with the matrix, accelerating localized corrosion. In contrast, under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the precipitates promote a more uniform and adherent Mg-oxide scale that enhances oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, thermally aged alloys will exhibit increased localized corrosion rates (due to galvanic effects) at ambient conditions but will show improved high-temperature oxidation resistance (via formation of a continuous protective oxide layer).
generation.baseline: The non-aged, as-cast metastable state with a relatively uniform elemental distribution and minimal intermetallic precipitate formation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is relevant for lightweight high-entropy alloys designed with density <6 g/cm³ and that inherently form both solid solution and intermetallic phases; it may not apply if complete homogenization occurs or if aging conditions exceed the limits where discrete precipitate formation is maintained.
generation.uncertainty: The exact size, volume fraction, and distribution of the Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates, and the quantitative impact on corrosion and oxidation rates, are not yet established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of the Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy from the same non-equilibrium process. One group is kept in the as-cast state while the other is subjected to controlled thermal aging at a moderate temperature designed to promote elemental partitioning. Perform detailed microstructural analysis (using SEM, TEM, and XRD) to detect the formation and distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. Conduct electrochemical corrosion tests at ambient temperature and high-temperature oxidation tests (tracking mass gain and oxide scale formation) on both groups.
measurements: Electrochemical corrosion testing (potentiodynamic polarization, impedance spectroscopy)
High-temperature oxidation kinetics (mass gain curves, oxide scale microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged samples do not show a significant formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates accompanied by worse corrosion performance at ambient conditions and improved high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Al-Ti-Containing Lightweight High-Entropy Alloys for Intermediate Temperature Applications

Abstract: AbstractIn this study, new high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which contain lightweight elements, namely Al and Ti, have been designed for intermediate temperature applications. Cr, Mo, and V were selected as the elements for the Al-Ti-containing HEAs by elemental screening using their binary phase diagrams. AlCrMoTi and AlCrMoTiV HEAs are confirmed as solid solutions with minor ordered B2 phases and have superb specific hardness when compared to that of commercial alloys. The present work demonstrates the desirable possibility for substitution of traditional materials that are applied at intermediate temperature to Al-Ti-containing lightweight HEAs.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, alloys design, lightweight alloys

Conclusions: In summary, HEAs which contained Al and Ti were designed based on their binary phase diagrams. This approach is powerful for screening candidate elements for novel HEAs.
